articles.title: Why Munya Chawawa is 'jumping ship' from social media to Shakespeare
articles.summary: The comedian is making his stage acting debut and says he wants to move away from social content.
articles.body:
Comedian, content creator and documentary maker Munya Chawawa became a star in the "golden era" of online video, but says his stage acting debut in Shakespeare is part of a move to "jump ship" from social media.

Recently, he has been immersing himself in footage of the UK's 1990s illegal rave scene.

It was a time of hedonism and freedom surrounded by political and media panic - and is the setting for a modern take on Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, in which Chawawa will appear.

"I've obviously done a super-deep dive into rave culture and watched loads of rave footage from all these little free parties where they would find an empty field," he says.

While some footage exists of those illicit outdoor parties, they came before everyone had phones and cameras - and Chawawa, 33, feels a pang of nostalgia for that age of analogue abandon.

"I absolutely miss an era where we were dancing for ourselves and not for a digital world somewhere," he says.

"We're all phone addicts," Chawawa continues. "The average person's picking up their phone 200 times a day. I'm on a bit of a conscious mission at the moment to reduce that.

"And interestingly, the top comments under all the videos I've been watching are people who were at those raves saying, 'I loved being able to dance, maybe get a little high, maybe get too sweaty for too long, and know there was no record of that.'"

Chawawa was in his teens when social media and smartphones took off, and says he "took for granted" the brief time before any and every fun occasion was recorded and posted for posterity.

If he ventures onto a dance floor now, he admits "my two-step has become a lot stiffer" out of anxiety that a wrong move could be filmed and send him viral.

"So yeah, I do definitely pine for those non-digital, in-person experiences, and I envy my parents for having them."

This is coming from someone who owes his fame to the digital age, after making his name with comic videos as characters like upper-class drill rapper Unknown P and chef Jonny Oliver.

But Chawawa has since branched out from social media - making two Bafta-nominated TV documentaries, starring on Taskmaster and doing stand-up comedy.

"I've been making my short-form satirical videos for almost eight years now, creeping up to a decade," he says. "I have a certain skill set that I've acquired there. It's skyrocketed me to all the places I wanted to go.

"But I suppose the question at the beginning was always - if these sketches do work and they do catapult me into this new stratosphere of entertainment, where am I trying to land?"

The aim, he says, was to land on "something bigger and onto a new challenge" - such as theatre acting.

He's starting by playing Bottom in Shakespeare's romantic caper A Midsummer Night's Dream at Chichester Festival Theatre in West Sussex.

In this 90s version, his character is a member of the Young Conservatives and is "a very political Bottom", he says, while Theseus is a Tory MP who has shut down free raves in the county.

"I take it super seriously and I'm very studious when we're in the room," Chawawa explains of his preparations. "I'm taking notes. I'm learning all of these mad Shakespeare terms like couplets and quatrains and anacreontics and stuff that definitely sounds made up but isn't.

"And I think also it's the perfect time to maybe... jump ship, I think is the right word.

"Social media platforms and their algorithms have very much angled themselves against the creatives at the moment, I think."

He's not jumping ship from social media completely, but says the online battle for eyeballs has "turned into a little bit of a dogfight, where even good stuff, even really consciously thought-out material, is just instantly swiped to the bottom of people's pages".

Chawawa thinks he was lucky to "enjoy the golden era of social media" before it became harder to cut through the noise.

"To be able to experiment, to be able to trial these characters and roll the dice on big ideas was fantastic because you were never getting lost in a sea of content.

"There's some mad statistic about there being tens of millions of videos uploaded a day now - but at the time it was like, 'I'm going to try this Jamie Oliver spoof or a Nigella [Lawson] character or the UK's first posh drill rapper, what do you think?' And it felt like the whole internet would give you feedback on that creative product."

He adds: "I love the fact that social media has allowed me to have a career in stand-up, as a documentarian and now as an actor, so I don't have any sort of resentment to it and how it's changed.

"But what I will say is I was there as the sun was coming up on social media, and it was very fun."

Chawawa fell in love with the theatre when he went to see The Lion King when he was 16 and realised it was like "the best movie you've ever seen, but in real life".

However, returning as an adult, he felt out of place as a black man. "In the shows I was going to, it didn't feel as though they were too welcoming to me being there, just through the small social cues."

He had a lightbulb moment after watching For Black Boys Who Have Considered Suicide When the Hue Gets Too Heavy by Ryan Calais Cameron, which "I still think is the best play I've ever seen". Chawawa found himself thinking, "I wish every black boy in the world could watch this play."

So he took a group of teenagers to watch it, which he describes as "the most fulfilling and magical and deeply moving experience".

Inspired by their reactions, Chawawa set up the Black Boys Theatre Club to take groups every month to plays ranging from Dracula to One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest - followed by a post-show discussion in Nando's.

"Every time we go and see a play, it's not about the boys skipping out of it going, 'I want to be the next Billy Elliot'," he says. "It's more just them realising it's a safe space for you. It can be your home if you want it to be. You will thrive on stage or as an audience member, but just know that theatre is a part of your multiverse."

In 2023, 10% of theatre audiences were from black, Asian or ethnically diverse backgrounds, according to Arts Council England data.

Chawawa praises theatres for opening their doors to the Black Boys Theatre Club and other efforts to attract more diverse audiences, but says lower ticket prices and "a societal shift" will make a bigger difference.

Next month, his club will travel to see him in A Midsummer Night's Dream - and he hopes more young minds will be captivated by the "snow globe of human emotion" that is live theatre.

"Really, truly, where else can I go in real life and watch somebody express all emotions without restraint? Sadness, anger, joy, envy. And I can be metres away, sometimes centimetres away from seeing real human emotion - not through a screen of any size, but in the room," he says.

"I believe that as more people do try and back off away from screens and digital experiences, theatre will experience a boom."

A Midsummer Night's Dream is at at Chichester Festival Theatre from 18 September to 17 October.

articles.body: 43-year-old British-Nigerian businessman and influencer R. Igho Ubiribo, who also went by the names Denisi or Ego, passed away earlier this year. The 43-year-old had been in Thailand in March for a luxury vacation and to get a cosmetic procedure done, after which he passed away. Here’s what we know so far about what happened to him.Igho Ubiribo passes away at 43TMZ reported that the famed influencer who hailed from Britain passed away in March earlier this year. The star had been traveling in Thailand at the time with his wife, Danielle Simba Allen, for a luxury vacation. During his stay in the country, Ubiribo decided to undergo a penile enlargement procedure. However, soon after the cosmetic surgery was done, the report revealed that he suffered from a fatal embolism.According to the reports and details shared by the Inner West London Coroner’s Court, the influencer had 40 milliliters of hyaluronic acid and lidocaine injected into him for the procedure. He and his wife had been staying at the Marriott hotel in Bangkok at the time, and after coming back from the procedure, they had gone to get massages. There, Igho complained of chest pain and passed out two times. He was taken to a nearby hospital for treatment; however, he lost consciousness before a CT scan could be taken. Medical personnel performed CPR and life-saving measures for more than 100 minutes; however, Igho passed away in the early hours of March 6. A statement from the report read, “Coroner Jean Harkin ruled that Igho died from a pulmonary embolism caused by the cosmetic procedure.”According to the outlet, the influencer was laid to rest in London, and his funeral was attended by friends and family members, as well as celebrities from the industry. Nigerian Afrobeats star Davido also attended his funeral and paid tribute to his friend.About Igho UbiriboIgho Ubiribo was a famed influencer and social media star who was known for leading an expensive life. articles.body: Yash's 'Toxic: A Fairytale For Grown-Ups' is entering a crucial phase at the box office. The challenge will be sustaining enough theatrical momentum to reach both milestones. The film's weekday slowdown and the growing competition from 'Mirzapur: The Movie' and 'Hanuman Ansh' make the next phase particularly important. Days 4 and 5 added Rs. 25.15 crore and Rs. 23 crore respectively, before collections eased further with Rs. 7.65 crore on Day 6 and Rs. 7.85 crore on Day 7. Day 8 brought in Rs. 5.10 crore, and Day 9 saw a further dip to Rs. 4.25 crore net, taking the film's India net total to Rs. 239.30 crore and its domestic gross to Rs. 285.70 crore by the end of its first nine days.The slowdown continued through the following days, with Day 10 bringing in Rs. 1.75 crore net across reduced shows, pushing the India gross to Rs. 287.75 crore and the India net total to Rs. 241.05 crore. Day 11 saw a mild uptick to Rs. 2.35 crore net, taking the domestic net past Rs. 243 crore. articles.title: Quote of the day by Bob Marley: 'None but ourselves can free our minds,' powerful life lesson explaining that the biggest battle can be within, from 'Redemption song' artist
articles.summary: The word freedom can have different meanings, and it is not always about politics, borders or breaking away from something physical. It has more to it.
articles.body: The word freedom can have different meanings, and it is not always about politics, borders or breaking away from something physical. It has more to it than what meets the eye. Fear, insecurity and the constant need for approval can leave a person feeling trapped even when nothing is physically stopping them. Bob Marley put that thought into words in his song 'Redemption Song'.Today's quote of the day by Bob Marley reads, “None but ourselves can free our minds.”What does the quote by Bob Marley mean?With these words, Marley conveyed the message that taking responsibility for our thoughts and choices is an important part of our lives. It is easy to blame circumstances when things do not work out. Sometimes, circumstances genuinely are difficult. But there are also moments when fear gets in the way before we have even tried.Imagine a man who wants to change his career, but can't, as he feels he is not good enough. Or someone who wants to speak up but fears getting judged and thus stays silent. The situation may not have changed, but the way that person sees themselves has become a barrier.That is where the quote becomes meaningful. Other people can encourage us and help us through difficult periods, but they cannot make every decision for us. At some point, we have to decide whether we are going to remain stuck in the same way of thinking or try to move past it.Of course, Marley was not saying that people can simply think their way out of every problem. Life does not work that way. Financial problems, difficult circumstances and personal struggles cannot always be solved by changing your attitude.But there is still something to be said for not allowing fear to make every decision.The thought also connects with 'Redemption Song', which became one of Marley’s most enduring songs. Released as part of the 1980 album 'Uprising', the track focuses heavily on freedom and liberation.Why is the quote by Bob Marley relevant today?The quote feels particularly familiar today, when people are constantly exposed to other people's lives. Social media has made comparison part of everyday life. Someone else's new job, holiday, relationship or achievement can make you question where you are in your own life. After a while, those comparisons can affect confidence.There is also the pressure to have everything figured out early. People are expected to know what career they want, what they should look like and where they should be in life. Falling behind can start feeling like failure.But nobody sees the complete picture of another person's life. Marley’s words highlight that being afraid of failure is normal. So is worrying about what people will say. The important part is not allowing those fears to make every choice for us.Sometimes, freeing your mind starts with something very ordinary — trying again, taking the opportunity you were unsure about or simply deciding that one mistake does not define you.Early Life of Bob MarleyBob Marley was born Robert Nesta Marley on February 6, 1945, in Nine Miles, Saint Ann Parish, Jamaica. He later moved to Kingston and spent part of his youth in Trench Town.Marley left school when he was 14 and briefly worked as a welder’s apprentice. Music remained his bigger interest, however, and he soon began pursuing it seriously.He started recording music in the early 1960s. He formed The Wailers with Bunny Wailer and Peter Tosh.Bob Marley’s rise to fameThe Wailers first established themselves in Jamaica. Soon they became a rage overseas. Their early association with producer Lee “Scratch” Perry helped develop their sound.There are several songs that helped them cater to the international audience; 'Catch a Fire', released in 1973, played an important role in introducing The Wailers to listeners outside Jamaica.More albums followed, including 'Burnin'', 'Natty Dread' and 'Exodus'. Marley gradually became one of reggae's most recognisable artists.Further, his songs addressed subjects such as inequality, spirituality, love, resistance and freedom. That combination helped his music travel across countries and generations.'Redemption Song' arrived on 'Uprising' in 1980. Unlike many of Marley’s reggae recordings, it was built around a much simpler acoustic arrangement, leaving the lyrics at the centre of the song.Marley passed away on May 11, 1981, aged 36. His career was cut short, but his music continued to grow in influence after his death.Decades later, “None but ourselves can free our minds” still works because it speaks to something most people understand. There are things in life we cannot control, but there are also fears and doubts that we have to confront ourselves. And sometimes, that is where real freedom begins.Give your child the gift of confidence! Claim your exclusive TOI Masterclass spot today!
